title: Technical English exam practice
description: Five observed CAT-II question formats, practised in paper order. The wording may change; the skills are the target.

sections.title: The two-part definition
sections.body: The photographed paper is a 90-minute, 50-mark CAT-II with five 10-mark questions. Its sequence is definitions, passage comprehension, a 100–120-word abstract, a conflict-management case, then a 200–250-word Statement of Purpose. The practice lessons keep that order, but one paper cannot guarantee future wording. Question 1 asks for five definitions (2 marks each). A complete technical definition names the word's class or category and then gives its distinguishing feature or function. Avoid circular wording, examples without a definition, and vague phrases such as “it is a thing.” The five words visible on this paper are Prototype, Recycling, Cybersecurity, Innovation and Sensor; the supplied word bank contains additional practice terms. Repeated entries in the bank are consolidated below.

sections.title: A reliable sentence frame
sections.body: [Term] is a [category] that [distinctive purpose or feature].

sections.title: The five words on the paper
items: Prototype — a preliminary model of a product or system, built to test its design or operation before final production.
Recycling — the process of collecting and processing used materials so they can be made into new products.
Cybersecurity — the practice of protecting computers, networks and data from unauthorized access, attack or damage.
Innovation — a new or improved idea, product or method put into practical use to solve a problem or create value.
Sensor — a device that detects a physical or environmental change and converts it into a signal or measurement.

sections.title: Build a full-mark definition
sections.body: Weak: “A sensor is used for sensing.” It repeats the word and gives no distinguishing function. Strong: “A sensor is a device that detects a physical or environmental change and converts it into a signal or measurement.” The first clause names the category (device); the rest explains what makes it useful. Practise aloud: define Prototype, Recycling, Cybersecurity, Innovation and Sensor without looking, then check that each answer contains both parts.

sections.title: Easy marks to protect
sections.body: Do not define a word with a synonym that is just as vague, give only an example, or confuse a category with a purpose. “A prototype is a product” is incomplete; say that it is a preliminary model used to test a design. The paper asks for the category and the distinguishing feature or function.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Use category + distinguishing feature/function. Keep one direct sentence, and check that it explains what the term is and what sets it apart.

sections.title: Answer from evidence, not memory
sections.body: The paper gives a passage about urban heat and reflective “cool roofs,” then asks four short questions worth 10 marks total (3, 3, 2 and 2 marks). Read the questions first, mark the sentence that answers each one, and separate a stated fact from an inference. For a 2-mark answer, give the relevant evidence and the point it supports; for a 3-mark inference, connect details and explain the conclusion. Do not add outside facts that the passage does not establish.

sections.title: A quick evidence routine
items: Circle the task word: infer, why, what type, or when.
Underline the exact evidence in the passage before writing.
Answer the question directly in the first sentence.
For an inference, state the evidence and then the conclusion it supports.
Keep each answer within the passage's limits; do not turn a cautious finding into a universal rule.

sections.title: Model answers for the cool-roof passage
sections.body: a) The treated roof surface became substantially cooler, and the top-floor rooms also became cooler, but the indoor change was smaller. This suggests that a cooler roof is associated with cooler rooms, while the effect indoors is reduced and is not a one-to-one temperature change. b) The result depends on local climate, shade, ventilation, insulation and building orientation; the benefit was more noticeable in sunny conditions. A cool roof is therefore one part of a broader strategy, not a universal fix. c) The treated roof used a high-reflectance material (light-coloured or specially coated) that reflected more incoming solar radiation. d) The reduction was most noticeable on sunny days. For full credit, answer each part separately and reuse the passage's precise qualifiers.

sections.title: Don't overclaim
sections.body: The passage reports measurements from two similar buildings during one hot period. It does not show that every cool roof will produce the same indoor change in every climate. Preserve words such as “can,” “may,” “smaller” and “most noticeable”; they set the limits of the evidence.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Quote or paraphrase the evidence, make only the inference it supports, and keep every qualifier. Answer all four subparts.

sections.title: Purpose · method · findings · conclusion
sections.body: The paper asks for an abstract of about 100–120 words and explicitly expects the purpose, method, major findings and conclusion in a clear academic style. An abstract is a compact account of a study, not a background essay or a list of headings. Use one connected paragraph unless the instructions request another format. Keep the reported observations and the conclusion distinct.

sections.title: Plan before drafting
items: Purpose: What question did the study examine?
Method: Who or what was observed, for how long, and which measures were collected?
Findings: What were the most important observed results?
Conclusion: What can the results support, and what limitation must remain?
Final check: Count words, keep an impersonal academic tone, and do not introduce results absent from the prompt.

sections.title: Worked abstract · classroom air-quality sensors
sections.body: Poor ventilation can affect classroom comfort, but routine checks may be costly. This study examined whether low-cost air-quality sensors could help staff identify rooms needing attention. Researchers monitored six classrooms for four weeks, recording carbon-dioxide concentration, temperature and humidity. They also noted class size and whether doors and windows were open. Carbon dioxide rose more quickly in crowded rooms when openings remained closed. Opening windows during breaks usually reduced levels within 15–25 minutes, while mechanically ventilated rooms showed more stable readings. These findings suggest that inexpensive sensors can support timely ventilation decisions. However, readings require periodic calibration, and the sensors cannot replace professional environmental assessment.

sections.title: Why the model works
items: Purpose: tests whether low-cost sensors can help identify rooms needing attention.
Method: names six classrooms, four weeks and the recorded conditions.
Findings: reports faster CO₂ rise in crowded, closed rooms and the observed ventilation patterns.
Conclusion and limit: sensors can support decisions, but need calibration and do not replace professional assessment.
The model is 105 words, within the requested 100–120-word range.

sections.title: Your turn · practise the same skill
items: Without looking at the model, write a 100–120-word abstract for the sensor study in the question.
Underline your purpose, method, findings and conclusion; check that each appears.
Compare every factual claim with the question prompt, then count the words.

sections.title: Keep evidence and claims aligned
sections.body: Do not claim that the sensors “proved” a health improvement; the prompt reports environmental measurements, not health outcomes. Avoid first-person opinion, recommendations unsupported by the study, and a long general introduction that pushes out the method or results.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: In 100–120 words, cover purpose, method, findings and a proportionate conclusion. Count the words and retain the study's limitation.

sections.title: Diagnose before proposing
sections.body: The case is about a mobile-app launch: developers want an extra week to fix performance issues, while marketing has announced the launch date and fears loss of customer trust if it slips. Blame, defensiveness and irregular updates make the conflict worse. The answer has two jobs: identify causes and propose suitable strategies, then justify how the plan protects teamwork and project goals. Critique the process and competing constraints, not the character of either team.

sections.title: A practical resolution sequence
items: Name shared goals: a reliable app and honest communication with customers.
Hold a short facilitated meeting. Let each team explain its evidence and constraints without interruption.
Agree on the severity of performance defects using test results and clear release criteria.
Compare options: fix critical issues before release, stage a limited launch, or communicate a revised date if the risk remains unacceptable.
Assign an owner and deadline to every action; publish a brief daily status and decision log.
Escalate unresolved scope or date decisions to the project sponsor rather than allowing further blame.

sections.title: Worked response · analysis and justification
sections.body: The conflict has three main causes: the teams have competing priorities, marketing committed to a date before the performance risk was resolved, and poor updates allowed uncertainty to turn into blame. A facilitated meeting should begin with the shared goal of a dependable launch and customer trust. The developers should present test results and classify defects by severity; marketing should explain the customer and campaign impact of delay. The teams can then agree on minimum release criteria and compare a short extension with a staged launch. Each action needs one owner, a deadline and a daily written status. If the teams cannot agree on an acceptable risk, the project sponsor should make the scope/date decision. This plan replaces accusation with evidence, gives both teams a voice and protects quality. Clear criteria and updates also help the project communicate honestly with customers.

sections.title: Make both parts visible
items: Part (a): state causes from the case, then name concrete conflict-management strategies.
Part (b): connect each strategy to an outcome: trust, collaboration, product quality or project goals.
Use facts in the scenario. Do not assume the launch must be delayed or that marketing alone caused the problem.
Practice: hide the model and write two causes, three specific actions, and one sentence explaining how the plan protects the project.

sections.title: Avoid a vague “communicate better” answer
sections.body: A general call for teamwork earns little by itself. Say who meets, what evidence they review, how a decision is made, who owns each action and how progress is shared.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Causes → shared goal → evidence-based discussion → agreed options and owners → updates/escalation → explain how teamwork and delivery are protected.

sections.title: A clear 200–250-word structure
sections.body: The paper provides a profile of a final-year B.Tech student applying to a postgraduate programme in Sustainable and Intelligent Engineering Systems. The response must be a structured Statement of Purpose of about 200–250 words and include motivation, relevant preparation/experience, programme fit and realistic career goals. Treat the supplied profile as the evidence: connect each detail to the next step rather than inventing awards, grades or achievements.

sections.title: Four moves, one story
items: Motivation: identify the problem or experience that led to this field.
Preparation: select relevant study, project and internship evidence; explain what each taught you.
Programme fit: connect the programme's stated focus to a real learning need. Do not invent specific courses not named in the prompt.
Career goals: state a credible near-term role and a longer-term contribution related to sustainable engineering.
Conclusion: bring the motivation and goal together without repeating the entire essay.

sections.title: Worked SOP · based only on the supplied profile
sections.body:
My final-year studies have shown me how engineering decisions can affect both energy use and the reliability of everyday systems. I want to pursue postgraduate study in Sustainable and Intelligent Engineering Systems because I hope to design solutions that are efficient, measurable and practical to maintain. My coursework has also helped me ask how design choices can be evaluated against measured performance rather than intention alone.

My preparation includes studying programming, sensors, control systems and energy. I also completed a sensor-based energy-monitoring mini-project, which introduced me to collecting readings and using them to understand system performance. During an industrial internship, I observed energy-management practices and the practical constraints that engineers must consider when recommending changes. Together, these experiences have encouraged me to connect automation with sustainable engineering rather than treat them as separate interests.

The programme fits my goal of deepening this combination of knowledge. I hope to strengthen my ability to assess energy systems, interpret sensor data and develop responsible control strategies. After graduation, I aim to begin in an engineering role involving energy monitoring or building systems, where I can learn from experienced teams and contribute to evidence-based improvements. In the longer term, I hope to lead projects that make energy use more efficient without overlooking reliability, cost or the people who operate the systems.

sections.title: Check the sample against the brief
items: The model is 217 words, within 200–250.
Motivation: links efficient, reliable systems to the applicant's interests.
Preparation: uses only the programming, sensors, control systems, energy, mini-project and internship details supplied.
Programme fit: explains the desired combination without inventing course names or facilities.
Goals: begins with a realistic engineering role and extends to a longer-term contribution.

sections.title: Your turn · draft before memorizing
items: Cover the model and write your own 200–250-word response using only the profile in the paper.
Mark each paragraph: motivation, preparation/experience, programme fit, or career goals.
Replace generic claims with a real detail from the profile and explain what you learned from it.
Use the model as a structure check, not as a script to reproduce.

sections.title: Keep it specific and truthful
sections.body: Do not turn the SOP into a résumé list, claim experience that is not in the profile, flatter the institution with generic phrases, or promise an unrealistic job title immediately after graduation. Explain what an experience taught you and how it prepares you for the stated programme.

sections.title: 30-second recap
sections.body: Motivation → relevant preparation with reflection → programme fit → realistic career goals. Use the profile's facts, keep a connected first-person voice and stay within 200–250 words.

questions.prompt: Which definition best follows the paper's “category + distinguishing feature or function” instruction?
options: A sensor is something that senses things.
A sensor is a device that detects a physical change and converts it into a signal or measurement.
A sensor is used in buildings.
A sensor is like a thermometer.
questions.explanation: It names the category (device) and explains the distinguishing function. The other options are circular, vague or only examples.

questions.prompt: Which detail distinguishes a prototype from a finished product?
options: It is a preliminary model used to test or refine a design.
It is always made from recycled material.
It is a device that measures temperature.
It is a legal right granted to an inventor.
questions.explanation: A prototype is an early model for testing and refinement. Recycled materials are not required; the other choices describe different terms.

questions.prompt: A strong definition of “recycling” should identify it as:
options: A product made from plastic.
A process that collects and processes used materials to make new products.
A device for measuring waste.
A law that bans every disposable item.
questions.explanation: This names recycling as a process and states its defining purpose without adding an unsupported universal claim.

questions.prompt: In the cool-roof passage, what does the comparison say about indoor temperature?
options: Indoor rooms cooled by exactly the same amount as the roof.
The treated roof surface was substantially cooler; top-floor rooms also cooled, but by a smaller amount.
The roof had no effect on the rooms.
Every floor cooled equally in all weather.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly distinguishes the larger roof-surface reduction from the smaller indoor difference.

questions.prompt: Why does the passage avoid calling cool roofs a universal solution?
options: The material cannot reflect sunlight.
The benefit depends on factors such as climate, shade, insulation, ventilation and building orientation.
The study measured no temperatures.
Cool roofs only work at night.
questions.explanation: The passage names contextual factors and recommends cool roofs as one part of a broader strategy.

questions.prompt: On which days was the temperature reduction most noticeable?
options: Cloudy days
Rainy days
Sunny days
The passage does not compare weather.
questions.explanation: The passage states that the reduction was most noticeable on sunny days and less pronounced during cloudy periods.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best covers the abstract requirements in the paper?
options: Opinion, history, quotation, recommendation
Purpose, method, major findings, conclusion
Title, references, acknowledgements, appendix
Problem, unrelated anecdote, personal response, slogan
questions.explanation: The prompt explicitly asks for the purpose, method, major findings and conclusion in an academic abstract.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is supported by the classroom sensor study?
options: Low-cost sensors can support timely ventilation decisions but need calibration and cannot replace professional assessment.
Low-cost sensors permanently eliminate poor ventilation.
The study proves that ventilation prevents every illness.
Professional environmental assessment is unnecessary.
questions.explanation: This matches both the reported conclusion and its limits; the other options overstate the findings.

questions.prompt: What is the requested length for the abstract?
options: About 50–60 words
About 100–120 words
About 200–250 words
No length is given
questions.explanation: Question 3 asks for an abstract of about 100–120 words.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful first step in the app-launch conflict?
options: Decide that marketing is always right.
Bring both teams together around a shared goal and review the evidence and constraints.
Cancel the project without discussion.
Ask each team to send more blame-focused emails.
questions.explanation: A facilitated, evidence-based discussion lets both teams explain their constraints before choosing a resolution.

questions.prompt: Which plan best protects teamwork and project goals?
options: Set clear release criteria, assign owners and deadlines, and share regular status updates.
Hide performance issues from customers and the project sponsor.
Let the teams continue working without agreed priorities.
Measure success only by keeping the original date.
questions.explanation: Shared criteria and accountable updates reduce uncertainty while balancing reliability, schedule and customer trust.

questions.prompt: Why should the teams classify defects using test results?
options: It replaces all communication.
It gives them a shared evidence base for judging launch risk and comparing options.
It guarantees that no delay will occur.
It proves one team is at fault.
questions.explanation: Evidence helps the teams assess severity and make a joint decision instead of relying on blame or assumptions.

questions.prompt: Which set contains all four required SOP elements in Question 5?
options: Motivation, relevant preparation/experience, programme fit and realistic career goals
Family history, unrelated hobbies, quotations and salary demand
Only grades and a list of subjects
A technical abstract and a reference list
questions.explanation: The paper explicitly lists motivation, relevant preparation/experience, programme fit and realistic career goals.

questions.prompt: What is the requested length for the SOP?
options: About 100–120 words
About 200–250 words
Exactly 500 words
No word range is given
questions.explanation: Question 5 requests a structured SOP of about 200–250 words.

questions.prompt: Which SOP sentence makes the strongest use of the supplied mini-project profile?
options: I have always been the best student in my university.
My sensor-based energy-monitoring project introduced me to collecting readings and using them to understand system performance.
I will immediately become the world's leading engineer.
I enjoy every subject and have no particular career goal.
questions.explanation: It uses a fact supplied in the profile and explains what the experience contributed, without inventing achievements.
